**`cancer_statistics_2025_rewrite.md`**

### 完成情况总结

- **原始论文**：Siegel RL et al., *Cancer statistics, 2025*, CA Cancer J Clin, 2025;75(1):10-45. DOI: 10.3322/caac.21871, PMCID: PMC11745215 (开放获取, CC BY-NC-ND).
- **全文获取**：已通过 NCBI PMC 成功获取原始全文，所有方法、数值、局限性和结论均来源于可核验原文。

### 重写正文结构

| 章节 | 核心可核验内容 |
|---|---|
| **摘要** | 204万新发病例/62万死亡预测；34%死亡率下降；AIAN/Black disparity；男女发病率趋同；肺癌发病率女性反超 |
| **引言** | 癌症为第二死因；COVID-19延迟诊断的后果；筛查恢复不平等 |
| **方法** | SEER/NPCR/NAACCR数据源；Joinpoint回归；两步法预测模型；延迟调整；AIAN种族分类校正 |
| **结果** | 各癌种发病和死亡数据（Table 1）；发病率趋势（M:F比率1.6→1.1；50岁以下女性高出82%）；死亡率趋势（4.5百万避免死亡）；种族差异（AIAN肾脏肝癌死亡白人的2-3倍）；儿童青少年癌症（5年生存率85%/87%） |
| **讨论** | 六种前十癌症发病率上升；种族差异归因于结构性障碍；COVID-19对诊断的影响 |
| **局限性** | 模型预测不可用于时间趋势比较；方法学迭代；AIAN城市人群排除；缺乏LGBTQ+数据 |
| **结论** | 死亡率持续下降但受制于年轻化、女性化和种族不平等 |

## ABSTRACT

Each year, the American Cancer Society estimates the numbers of new cancer cases and deaths in the United States and compiles the most recent data on population‐based cancer occurrence and outcomes using incidence data collected by central cancer registries (through 2021) and mortality data collected by the National Center for Health Statistics (through 2022). In 2025, 2,041,910 new cancer cases and 618,120 cancer deaths are projected to occur in the United States. The cancer mortality rate continued to decline through 2022, averting nearly 4.5 million deaths since 1991 because of smoking reductions, earlier detection for some cancers, and improved treatment. Yet alarming disparities persist; Native American people bear the highest cancer mortality, including rates that are two to three times those in White people for kidney, liver, stomach, and cervical cancers. Similarly, Black people have two‐fold higher mortality than White people for prostate, stomach, and uterine corpus cancers. Overall cancer incidence has generally declined in men but has risen in women, narrowing the male‐to‐female rate ratio (RR) from a peak of 1.6 (95% confidence interval, 1.57–1.61) in 1992 to 1.1 (95% confidence interval, 1.12–1.12) in 2021. However, rates in women aged 50–64 years have already surpassed those in men (832.5 vs. 830.6 per 100,000), and younger women (younger than 50 years) have an 82% higher incidence rate than their male counterparts (141.1 vs. 77.4 per 100,000), up from 51% in 2002. Notably, lung cancer incidence in women surpassed that in men among people younger than 65 years in 2021 (15.7 vs. 15.4 per 100,000; RR, 0.98, *p* = 0.03). In summary, cancer mortality continues to decline, but future gains are threatened by rampant racial inequalities and a growing burden of disease in middle‐aged and young adults, especially women. Continued progress will require investment in cancer prevention and access to equitable treatment, especially for Native American and Black individuals.

**Keywords:** cancer cases, cancer statistics, death rates, incidence, mortality

## INTRODUCTION

Cancer is the second leading cause of death in the United States overall and the leading cause among people younger than 85 years. The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID‐19) pandemic caused delays in the diagnosis and treatment of cancer in 2020 because of health care setting closures, loss of employment and health insurance, and fear of COVID‐19 exposure. [1](#caac21871-bib-0001) , [2](#caac21871-bib-0002) The extent to which these delays lead to increased diagnosis of advanced‐stage disease and higher cancer mortality will be revealed gradually over many years. A recent modeling study estimated 4000 to 7000 excess deaths from colorectal cancer (CRC) by 2040, depending on the speed of screening recovery. [3](#caac21871-bib-0003) What is already established is the disproportionate direct and indirect impact of the pandemic on communities of color, [4](#caac21871-bib-0004) , [5](#caac21871-bib-0005) including slower recovery of cancer screening, [6](#caac21871-bib-0006) which will likely exacerbate existing cancer disparities.

In this article, we provide the estimated numbers of new cancer cases and deaths in 2025 in the United States nationally and for each state as well as a comprehensive overview of cancer occurrence based on up‐to‐date, population‐based data for cancer incidence and mortality through 2021 and 2022, respectively. We also estimate the total number of cancer deaths averted through 2022 because of the continuous decline in the cancer death rate over the past several decades.

## MATERIALS AND METHODS

### Data sources

Population‐based cancer incidence data in the United States have been collected by the National Cancer Institute's (NCI's) Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) program since 1973 and by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's (CDC's) National Program of Cancer Registries (NPCR) since 1995. The SEER program is the only source for historic population‐based incidence data from the eight oldest SEER areas (Connecticut, Hawaii, Iowa, New Mexico, Utah, and the metropolitan areas of Atlanta, San Francisco‐Oakland, and Seattle‐Puget Sound), representing approximately 8% of the US population. [7](#caac21871-bib-0007) Historical survival data (1975–1977 and 1995–1997) are based on the SEER 8 areas plus the Detroit metropolitan area, as published previously. [8](#caac21871-bib-0008) Contemporary survival statistics are based on data from the SEER 8 registries plus the Alaska Native Tumor Registry and the registries in California, Georgia, Idaho, Kentucky, Louisiana, New Jersey, New York, and Texas, [9](#caac21871-bib-0009) representing 42% of the US population, with vital status follow‐up through 2021. All 22 SEER registries (with the addition of Massachusetts and Illinois), covering 48% of the United States, were the source for the probability of developing cancer.

The North American Association of Central Cancer Registries (NAACCR) compiles and reports incidence data from 1995 forward for registries that participate in the SEER program and/or the NPCR. These data approach 100% coverage of the US population for the most recent years and were the source for the projected new cancer cases in 2025, contemporary incidence trends, cross‐sectional incidence rates, and stage distribution. [10](#caac21871-bib-0010) , [11](#caac21871-bib-0011) The incidence data presented herein differ slightly from those published online in the NAACCR's Cancer in North America (CiNA) Explorer ([apps.naaccr.org/explorer/](http://apps.naaccr.org/explorer/), September 1, 2024) because rates are adjusted for delays in case reporting using national delay factors. Incidence data for Puerto Rico were abstracted from the CiNA Explorer.

Mortality data from 1930 to 2022 were provided by the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS). [12](#caac21871-bib-0012) , [13](#caac21871-bib-0013) Forty‐seven states and the District of Columbia met data quality requirements for reporting to the national vital statistics system in 1930, and Texas, Alaska, and Hawaii began reporting in 1933, 1959, and 1960, respectively. The methods for abstraction and age‐adjustment of mortality data before 1969 are described elsewhere. [13](#caac21871-bib-0013) , [14](#caac21871-bib-0014) Contemporary 5‐year mortality rates for Puerto Rico were obtained from State Cancer Profiles ([statecancerprofiles.cancer.gov](http://statecancerprofiles.cancer.gov), August 1, 2024), a collaboration between the CDC and the NCI.

All cancer cases were classified according to the *International Classification of Diseases for Oncology*, third edition, except childhood and adolescent cancers, which were classified according to the *International Classification of Childhood Cancer*. [15](#caac21871-bib-0015) , [16](#caac21871-bib-0016) , [17](#caac21871-bib-0017) Causes of death were classiﬁed according to the *International Classiﬁcation of Diseases*. [18](#caac21871-bib-0018)

### Statistical analysis

#### Incidence and mortality

All incidence and death rates were age standardized to the 2000 US standard population (19 age groups) and expressed per 100,000 persons (or per million for childhood and adolescent cancer incidence), as calculated by the NCI's SEER\*Stat software, version 8.4.2. Population data were modified intercensal annual county estimates by age, sex, race, and Hispanic origin produced by the US Census Bureau and the NCHS with support from the NCI except for 2010–2019 data, which were produced by Woods & Poole Economics, Inc. through a contract with the NCI, and 2020–2022 data, which were based on Vintage 2022 estimates. Official US Census Bureau intercensal population estimates are anticipated to be released in fall 2024 and will be incorporated into 2025 data releases ([https://seer.cancer.gov/popdata/](https://seer.cancer.gov/popdata/), September 1, 2024). Population estimates incorporate race‐bridging, which combines multiple‐race categories in the 2000 and 2010 census into individual race categories. For more information on population estimates issued by the US Census Bureau, see [census.gov/programs‐surveys/popest/guidance.html](http://census.gov/programs-surveys/popest/guidance.html), July 1, 2024.

The probability of developing cancer was calculated using the NCI's DevCan software, version 6.9.1, and the annual percent change (APC) in rates was quantified using the NCI's Joinpoint Regression Program, version 5.2.0. Trends were described as increasing or decreasing when the APC was statistically significant based on a two‐sided *p* value < .05, calculated using the parametric method, and otherwise were described as stable. Trend and lifetime risk analyses exclude cancer incidence in 2020 because the Joinpoint and DevCan modeling programs were not designed to accommodate such a large, single‐year data anomaly as occurred because of pandemic‐related disruptions in health care. [19](#caac21871-bib-0019)

All statistics presented by race are exclusive of Hispanic ethnicity for reduced racial misclassification. Racial misclassification for the American Indian and Alaska Native (AIAN) population was further mitigated by restricting incidence rates to Purchased/Referred Care Delivery Area counties and adjusting nationally representative mortality rates using classification ratios previously published by the NCHS. [20](#caac21871-bib-0020) Life tables by Hispanic ethnicity were published in 2018 and were used for relative survival comparisons between White and Black individuals. [21](#caac21871-bib-0021)

Whenever possible, cancer incidence rates were adjusted for delays in reporting, which occur because of lags in case capture and data corrections. Delay adjustment has the largest effect on the most recent data years and for cancers that are frequently diagnosed in outpatient settings (e.g., melanoma, leukemia, and prostate cancer). For example, the leukemia incidence rate for 2021 was 13% higher after adjusting for reporting delays (15.4 vs. 13.6 per 100,000 persons). Delay adjustment is particularly important when quantifying contemporary trends. [22](#caac21871-bib-0022)

#### Projected cancer cases and deaths in 2025

The most recent year for which incidence and mortality data are available lags 2–3 years behind the current year because of the time required for data collection, compilation, quality control, and dissemination. Therefore, we project the numbers of new cancer cases and deaths in the United States in 2025 to estimate the contemporary cancer burden using two‐step statistical modeling described in detail elsewhere. [23](#caac21871-bib-0023) , [24](#caac21871-bib-0024) Briefly, complete cancer diagnoses were estimated for every state from 2007 through 2021 based on high‐quality, delay‐adjusted incidence data from 50 states and the District of Columbia (99.7% population coverage) and state‐level variations in sociodemographic characteristics, lifestyle factors, medical settings, and cancer screening behaviors. [25](#caac21871-bib-0025) Counts were adjusted for the deficit in cases during March through May 2020 because of the COVID‐19 pandemic based on the proportion of cases diagnosed in those months in previous years. Modeled state and national counts were then projected 4 years ahead using a novel, data‐driven Joinpoint algorithm. [24](#caac21871-bib-0024) Basal cell and squamous cell skin cancers cannot be estimated because these diagnoses are not recorded by most cancer registries.

# Cancer Statistics, 2025: A Structured Rewrite

**Source:** Siegel RL, Kratzer TB, Giaquinto AN, Sung H, Jemal A. Cancer statistics, 2025. *CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians*. 2025;75(1):10–45.

- **DOI:** [10.3322/caac.21871](https://doi.org/10.3322/caac.21871)
- **PMID:** [39817679](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39817679/)
- **PMCID:** [PMC11745215](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11745215/)
- **License:** CC BY-NC-ND 4.0

---

## Abstract

The American Cancer Society annually projects the incidence and mortality burden of cancer in the United States using population-based surveillance data. In 2025, an estimated 2,041,910 new invasive cancer cases and 618,120 cancer deaths are anticipated. While the overall cancer death rate has dropped by 34% from its 1991 peak — corresponding to approximately 4.5 million averted deaths — substantial racial disparities and shifting demographic patterns raise concern. American Indian and Alaska Native populations experience the highest overall cancer mortality, with rates two to three times those of White individuals for kidney, liver, stomach, and cervical cancers. The male-to-female incidence rate ratio has contracted from 1.6 in 1992 to 1.1 in 2021, driven by declining rates in men and rising rates in women; incidence among women younger than 50 years is now 82% higher than in their male counterparts. Lung cancer incidence in women surpassed that in men among those younger than 65 years for the first time in 2021. The growing burden of disease in middle-aged and younger adults, especially women, and enduring racial inequities threaten recent progress.

---

## Introduction

Cancer remains the second leading cause of death in the United States overall and the leading cause for persons under 85 years of age. The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted screening, diagnosis, and treatment in 2020 through health care closures, loss of insurance coverage, and reduced care-seeking; modeling suggests 4,000–7,000 excess colorectal cancer deaths by 2040 attributable to those disruptions. Communities of color bore a disproportionate burden of the pandemic's indirect effects, including slower recovery of cancer screening, which will likely widen pre-existing disparities. This report presents nationally and state-level estimates of new cancer cases and deaths for 2025, incidence and mortality trends through 2021 and 2022, respectively, and an accounting of deaths averted as a result of the sustained decline in cancer mortality over the past three decades.

---

## Methods

### Data Sources

Incidence data were drawn from the National Cancer Institute's Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) program and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's National Program of Cancer Registries (NPCR), compiled by the North American Association of Central Cancer Registries (NAACCR). These data approach complete coverage of the U.S. population. Historical incidence trends and survival estimates used the eight original SEER registries (approximately 8% of the population), whereas contemporary survival relied on an expanded 17-registry set (42% coverage). Mortality records from 1930 through 2022 were obtained from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS). Case classification followed the *International Classification of Diseases for Oncology*, third edition; childhood cancers used the *International Classification of Childhood Cancer*. Puerto Rico incidence and mortality data came from CiNA Explorer and State Cancer Profiles, respectively.

### Statistical Procedures

All rates were age-standardized to the 2000 U.S. standard population and expressed per 100,000 person-years (per million for pediatric cancers). Annual percent change (APC) was calculated by Joinpoint regression (version 5.2.0), with statistical significance set at two-sided *p* < 0.05. Incidence rates were delay-adjusted to account for reporting lags; 2020 incidence data were excluded from trend and lifetime-risk analyses because the pandemic created a single-year anomaly incompatible with Joinpoint and DevCan assumptions.

### Projections for 2025

A two-step modeling approach projected 2025 case and death counts. First, complete diagnoses for 2007–2021 were modeled from delay-adjusted NAACCR data (50 states plus the District of Columbia, 99.7% coverage), incorporating state-level sociodemographic factors, lifestyle variables, and screening behaviors. The March–May 2020 deficit was corrected using historical monthly proportions. Second, modeled counts were projected four years forward via a data-driven Joinpoint algorithm. Death projections applied the same algorithm to 2008–2022 reported mortality.

### Estimation of Averted Deaths

The number of cancer deaths avoided was calculated as the cumulative annual difference between observed deaths and those expected had the age-specific death rates of the peak year (1990 for men, 1991 for women) persisted through 2022.

### Race and Ethnicity Data

All statistics by race exclude Hispanic ethnicity to reduce misclassification. For the American Indian and Alaska Native (AIAN) population, incidence rates were further restricted to Purchased/Referred Care Delivery Area counties, and nationally representative mortality rates were corrected using NCHS classification ratios.

---

## Results

### Projected Burden for 2025

An estimated 2,041,910 new invasive cancer diagnoses are expected in the United States in 2025, corresponding to roughly 5,600 cases daily. In addition, approximately 59,080 cases of female breast ductal carcinoma in situ and 107,240 cases of melanoma in situ are anticipated. The lifetime probability of developing invasive cancer is 39.9% for men and 39.0% for women.

The three most commonly diagnosed invasive cancers are projected to be prostate (313,780), female breast (316,950), and lung and bronchus (226,650), followed by colorectal (154,270), melanoma of the skin (104,960), and urinary bladder (84,870). The leading causes of cancer death are projected to be lung and bronchus (124,730), colorectal (52,900), pancreas (51,980), female breast (42,170), and prostate (35,770).

### Incidence Trends

From 1975 to 2021, overall cancer incidence moved in divergent directions by sex: rates in men have generally decreased, while rates in women rose from 361.2 per 100,000 (1978) to 443.2 (2021), a 23% increase. The male-to-female rate ratio narrowed from 1.6 (95% CI, 1.57–1.61) in 1992 to 1.1 (95% CI, 1.12–1.12) in 2021. Among adults 50–64 years, incidence rates have already converged (832.5 for women vs. 830.6 for men per 100,000). In the under-50 age group, women had an 82% greater incidence rate than men in 2021 (141.1 vs. 77.4 per 100,000), up from 51% in 2002, driven largely by breast and thyroid cancers. Lung cancer incidence among persons younger than 65 crossed over in 2021, with rates higher in women than in men for the first time (15.7 vs. 15.4 per 100,000; rate ratio, 0.98; *p* = 0.03).

Over the most recent decade (2012–2021), female breast cancer incidence increased 1% per year overall, with the fastest rise in women under 50 (1.4% annually) and in Hispanic (1.6%) and Asian American/Pacific Islander (2.6%) women. Uterine corpus cancer increased approximately 1% per year since the mid-2000s. Colorectal cancer incidence in adults under 50 rose 2.4% per year; among those 50–64, rates increased 0.4% annually, while rates in persons 65 and older declined. Thyroid cancer incidence decreased 2% per year since 2014, reflecting deliberate efforts to reduce overdiagnosis. Cervical cancer rates among women aged 30–44 years rose 11% from 2013 to 2021. Melanoma and liver cancer rates have stabilized in men but continue to increase in women by approximately 2% per year.

### Mortality Trends

The overall cancer death rate has fallen 34% from 1991 through 2022, translating to nearly 4.5 million averted cancer deaths (3,021,200 in men and 1,437,500 in women). Lung cancer mortality dropped 61% from the 1990 peak in men and 38% from the 2002 peak in women. Colorectal cancer death rates declined 55% in men since 1980 and 60% in women since 1969. Female breast cancer mortality decreased 44% from its 1989 peak, avoiding more than 517,900 deaths. Prostate cancer mortality in 2022 was 52% lower than the 1993 peak. Recent accelerations in the pace of decline were noted for lung cancer (to nearly 5% per year in men and 4% in women since 2013/2014).

Conversely, pancreatic cancer death rates have increased steadily since the 1930s. Uterine corpus cancer mortality continues to rise at 1.5% per year (2013–2022). Liver cancer mortality has reversed direction in men (declining 1.2% per year from 2018–2022) but continues to climb in women (0.7% per year).

### Racial and Ethnic Disparities

Cancer incidence and mortality vary markedly by race and ethnicity. AIAN populations bear the highest overall cancer mortality and the highest mortality from colorectal, kidney, liver, lung, stomach, and cervical cancers. Black men have the highest prostate cancer mortality, ranging from two to four times that of any other group. Black women have the highest breast and uterine corpus cancer death rates, with the latter two to three times higher than in all other women. Hispanic and Asian American/Pacific Islander populations suffer liver cancer mortality approximately 40%–50% higher and stomach cancer mortality twice as high as White individuals.

Differences in stage at diagnosis and care delivery contribute to these patterns. Only 56% of uterine corpus cancers and 58% of breast cancers in Black women are found at localized stage, versus 71% and 68% in White women. Black women are half as likely as White women to receive guideline-concordant diagnostic procedures for uterine corpus cancer. In 2022, 25% of AIAN individuals lived below the federal poverty level, as did 17% of Black and Hispanic individuals, compared with 9% of White and Asian individuals.

### Childhood and Adolescent Cancer

In 2025, approximately 9,550 children (0–14 years) and 5,140 adolescents (15–19 years) are projected to receive a cancer diagnosis, with 1,050 and 600 deaths, respectively. The cumulative risk of cancer before age 20 is 1 in 264. Leukemia accounts for 28% of childhood cancers, followed by central nervous system tumors (27%); in adolescents, central nervous system tumors predominate (22%).

Cancer mortality among children fell from 6.3 to 1.9 per 100,000 (70% reduction) and among adolescents from 7.2 to 2.7 per 100,000 (63% reduction) since 1970. Leukemia-specific mortality declined 83% in children and 73% in adolescents. Five-year relative survival for all cancers improved from 58% in the mid-1970s to 85% during 2014–2020 for children, and from 68% to 87% for adolescents.

---

## Discussion

This report documents a 34% overall decline in U.S. cancer mortality from 1991 through 2022, driven primarily by tobacco control, advances in early detection for selected malignancies, and therapeutic progress — particularly targeted therapy and immunotherapy in recent years. These gains have collectively prevented nearly 4.5 million deaths.

However, the data also reveal an unsettling shift in the demographic profile of cancer. Incidence is rising for six of the ten most common cancers (breast, prostate, melanoma, uterine corpus, pancreas, and colorectal cancer in persons under 65), and two of these predominantly affect women. As a result, the incidence excess historically observed in men has largely disappeared, with women in the 50–64 age group now statistically tied and younger women far outpacing their male peers. The convergence of lung cancer incidence below age 65 underscores that historical female advantage in smoking-related cancers has eroded.

The racial disparities documented in this report are stark and persistent. AIAN populations experience the highest mortality across multiple cancer types, and Black individuals continue to face substantially elevated death rates for potentially preventable or screen-detectable cancers. Lower stage at diagnosis and differential access to guideline-concordant care — compounded by higher poverty rates — point to structural barriers rather than biological differences as the primary drivers of these gaps.

The pandemic-era interruption of cancer care constitutes an additional concern. The large deficit in 2020 diagnoses was concentrated among asymptomatic, early-stage disease, and the lack of a compensatory "catch-up" in 2021 data (except for breast cancer) suggests genuine delays in detection with possible downstream effects on stage distribution and survival. Published modeling of 4,000–7,000 excess colorectal cancer deaths through 2040 illustrates the time scale on which these consequences may unfold.

The favorable trends in childhood and adolescent cancer survival represent a sustained achievement of pediatric oncology, with 5-year survival now exceeding 85%. Nonetheless, incidence continues to rise slowly in adolescents, warranting continued etiologic investigation.

---

## Limitations

This report has several important limitations acknowledged in the source manuscript. Estimated case and death counts for 2025 are model-based, three- to four-year forward projections; they cannot substitute for observed incidence and mortality rates for tracking temporal change. The projection methodology has been updated periodically, most recently in 2021, limiting the comparability of estimates across annual editions. The models are sensitive to abrupt fluctuations in observed data and cannot account for unanticipated changes in detection or clinical practice.

Racial and ethnic misclassification in medical records and death certificates systematically undercounts cancer events in non-White populations. To mitigate this, AIAN incidence rates are confined to Purchased/Referred Care Delivery Area counties, a restriction that excludes roughly one third of the AIAN population residing in urban areas. Broad racial and ethnic groupings mask heterogeneity within categories; combined AAPI data, for instance, obscure markedly worse outcomes among Pacific Islander individuals. The absence of sexual orientation and gender identity data in cancer surveillance completely precludes analysis of the LGBTQ+ population.

---

## Conclusion

U.S. cancer mortality continues to decline, yielding a 34% reduction relative to the 1991 peak and approximately 4.5 million deaths averted. # Cancer Statistics, 2025: A Structured Rewrite

**Source:** Siegel RL, Kratzer TB, Giaquinto AN, Sung H, Jemal A. Cancer statistics, 2025. *CA: A Cancer Journal for Clinicians*. 2025;75(1):10–45.

- **DOI:** [10.3322/caac.21871](https://doi.org/10.3322/caac.21871)
- **PMID:** [39817679](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39817679/)
- **PMCID:** [PMC11745215](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11745215/)
- **License:** CC BY-NC-ND 4.0

---

## Abstract

The American Cancer Society annually projects the incidence and mortality burden of cancer in the United States using population-based surveillance data. In 2025, an estimated 2,041,910 new invasive cancer cases and 618,120 cancer deaths are anticipated. While the overall cancer death rate has dropped by 34% from its 1991 peak — corresponding to approximately 4.5 million averted deaths — substantial racial disparities and shifting demographic patterns raise concern. American Indian and Alaska Native populations experience the highest overall cancer mortality, with rates two to three times those of White individuals for kidney, liver, stomach, and cervical cancers. The male-to-female incidence rate ratio has contracted from 1.6 in 1992 to 1.1 in 2021, driven by declining rates in men and rising rates in women; incidence among women younger than 50 years is now 82% higher than in their male counterparts. Lung cancer incidence in women surpassed that in men among those younger than 65 years for the first time in 2021. The growing burden of disease in middle-aged and younger adults, especially women, and enduring racial inequities threaten recent progress.

---

## Introduction

Cancer remains the second leading cause of death in the United States overall and the leading cause for persons under 85 years of age. The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted screening, diagnosis, and treatment in 2020 through health care closures, loss of insurance coverage, and reduced care-seeking; modeling suggests 4,000–7,000 excess colorectal cancer deaths by 2040 attributable to those disruptions. Communities of color bore a disproportionate burden of the pandemic's indirect effects, including slower recovery of cancer screening, which will likely widen pre-existing disparities. This report presents nationally and state-level estimates of new cancer cases and deaths for 2025, incidence and mortality trends through 2021 and 2022, respectively, and an accounting of deaths averted as a result of the sustained decline in cancer mortality over the past three decades.

---

## Methods

### Data Sources

Incidence data were drawn from the National Cancer Institute's Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) program and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's National Program of Cancer Registries (NPCR), compiled by the North American Association of Central Cancer Registries (NAACCR). These data approach complete coverage of the U.S. population. Historical incidence trends and survival estimates used the eight original SEER registries (approximately 8% of the population), whereas contemporary survival relied on an expanded 17-registry set (42% coverage). Mortality records from 1930 through 2022 were obtained from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS). Case classification followed the *International Classification of Diseases for Oncology*, third edition; childhood cancers used the *International Classification of Childhood Cancer*. Puerto Rico incidence and mortality data came from CiNA Explorer and State Cancer Profiles, respectively.

### Statistical Procedures

All rates were age-standardized to the 2000 U.S. standard population and expressed per 100,000 person-years (per million for pediatric cancers). Annual percent change (APC) was calculated by Joinpoint regression (version 5.2.0), with statistical significance set at two-sided *p* < 0.05. Incidence rates were delay-adjusted to account for reporting lags; 2020 incidence data were excluded from trend and lifetime-risk analyses because the pandemic created a single-year anomaly incompatible with Joinpoint and DevCan assumptions.

### Projections for 2025

A two-step modeling approach projected 2025 case and death counts. First, complete diagnoses for 2007–2021 were modeled from delay-adjusted NAACCR data (50 states plus the District of Columbia, 99.7% coverage), incorporating state-level sociodemographic factors, lifestyle variables, and screening behaviors. The March–May 2020 deficit was corrected using historical monthly proportions. Second, modeled counts were projected four years forward via a data-driven Joinpoint algorithm. Death projections applied the same algorithm to 2008–2022 reported mortality.

### Estimation of Averted Deaths

The number of cancer deaths avoided was calculated as the cumulative annual difference between observed deaths and those expected had the age-specific death rates of the peak year (1990 for men, 1991 for women) persisted through 2022.

### Race and Ethnicity Data

All statistics by race exclude Hispanic ethnicity to reduce misclassification. For the American Indian and Alaska Native (AIAN) population, incidence rates were further restricted to Purchased/Referred Care Delivery Area counties, and nationally representative mortality rates were corrected using NCHS classification ratios.

---

## Results

### Projected Burden for 2025

An estimated 2,041,910 new invasive cancer diagnoses are expected in the United States in 2025, corresponding to roughly 5,600 cases daily. In addition, approximately 59,080 cases of female breast ductal carcinoma in situ and 107,240 cases of melanoma in situ are anticipated. The lifetime probability of developing invasive cancer is 39.9% for men and 39.0% for women.

The three most commonly diagnosed invasive cancers are projected to be prostate (313,780), female breast (316,950), and lung and bronchus (226,650), followed by colorectal (154,270), melanoma of the skin (104,960), and urinary bladder (84,870). The leading causes of cancer death are projected to be lung and bronchus (124,730), colorectal (52,900), pancreas (51,980), female breast (42,170), and prostate (35,770).

### Incidence Trends

From 1975 to 2021, overall cancer incidence moved in divergent directions by sex: rates in men have generally decreased, while rates in women rose from 361.2 per 100,000 (1978) to 443.2 (2021), a 23% increase. The male-to-female rate ratio narrowed from 1.6 (95% CI, 1.57–1.61) in 1992 to 1.1 (95% CI, 1.12–1.12) in 2021. Among adults 50–64 years, incidence rates have already converged (832.5 for women vs. 830.6 for men per 100,000). In the under-50 age group, women had an 82% greater incidence rate than men in 2021 (141.1 vs. 77.4 per 100,000), up from 51% in 2002, driven largely by breast and thyroid cancers. Lung cancer incidence among persons younger than 65 crossed over in 2021, with rates higher in women than in men for the first time (15.7 vs. 15.4 per 100,000; rate ratio, 0.98; *p* = 0.03).

Over the most recent decade (2012–2021), female breast cancer incidence increased 1% per year overall, with the fastest rise in women under 50 (1.4% annually) and in Hispanic (1.6%) and Asian American/Pacific Islander (2.6%) women. Uterine corpus cancer increased approximately 1% per year since the mid-2000s. Colorectal cancer incidence in adults under 50 rose 2.4% per year; among those 50–64, rates increased 0.4% annually, while rates in persons 65 and older declined. Thyroid cancer incidence decreased 2% per year since 2014, reflecting deliberate efforts to reduce overdiagnosis. Cervical cancer rates among women aged 30–44 years rose 11% from 2013 to 2021. Melanoma and liver cancer rates have stabilized in men but continue to increase in women by approximately 2% per year.

### Mortality Trends

The overall cancer death rate has fallen 34% from 1991 through 2022, translating to nearly 4.5 million averted cancer deaths (3,021,200 in men and 1,437,500 in women). Lung cancer mortality dropped 61% from the 1990 peak in men and 38% from the 2002 peak in women. Colorectal cancer death rates declined 55% in men since 1980 and 60% in women since 1969. Female breast cancer mortality decreased 44% from its 1989 peak, avoiding more than 517,900 deaths. Prostate cancer mortality in 2022 was 52% lower than the 1993 peak. Recent accelerations in the pace of decline were noted for lung cancer (to nearly 5% per year in men and 4% in women since 2013/2014).

Conversely, pancreatic cancer death rates have increased steadily since the 1930s. Uterine corpus cancer mortality continues to rise at 1.5% per year (2013–2022). Liver cancer mortality has reversed direction in men (declining 1.2% per year from 2018–2022) but continues to climb in women (0.7% per year).

### Racial and Ethnic Disparities

Cancer incidence and mortality vary markedly by race and ethnicity. AIAN populations bear the highest overall cancer mortality and the highest mortality from colorectal, kidney, liver, lung, stomach, and cervical cancers. Black men have the highest prostate cancer mortality, ranging from two to four times that of any other group. Black women have the highest breast and uterine corpus cancer death rates, with the latter two to three times higher than in all other women. Hispanic and Asian American/Pacific Islander populations suffer liver cancer mortality approximately 40%–50% higher and stomach cancer mortality twice as high as White individuals.

Differences in stage at diagnosis and care delivery contribute to these patterns. Only 56% of uterine corpus cancers and 58% of breast cancers in Black women are found at localized stage, versus 71% and 68% in White women. Black women are half as likely as White women to receive guideline-concordant diagnostic procedures for uterine corpus cancer. In 2022, 25% of AIAN individuals lived below the federal poverty level, as did 17% of Black and Hispanic individuals, compared with 9% of White and Asian individuals.

### Childhood and Adolescent Cancer

In 2025, approximately 9,550 children (0–14 years) and 5,140 adolescents (15–19 years) are projected to receive a cancer diagnosis, with 1,050 and 600 deaths, respectively. The cumulative risk of cancer before age 20 is 1 in 264. Leukemia accounts for 28% of childhood cancers, followed by central nervous system tumors (27%); in adolescents, central nervous system tumors predominate (22%).

Cancer mortality among children fell from 6.3 to 1.9 per 100,000 (70% reduction) and among adolescents from 7.2 to 2.7 per 100,000 (63% reduction) since 1970. Leukemia-specific mortality declined 83% in children and 73% in adolescents. Five-year relative survival for all cancers improved from 58% in the mid-1970s to 85% during 2014–2020 for children, and from 68% to 87% for adolescents.

---

## Discussion

This report documents a 34% overall decline in U.S. cancer mortality from 1991 through 2022, driven primarily by tobacco control, advances in early detection for selected malignancies, and therapeutic progress — particularly targeted therapy and immunotherapy in recent years. These gains have collectively prevented nearly 4.5 million deaths.

However, the data also reveal an unsettling shift in the demographic profile of cancer. Incidence is rising for six of the ten most common cancers (breast, prostate, melanoma, uterine corpus, pancreas, and colorectal cancer in persons under 65), and two of these predominantly affect women. As a result, the incidence excess historically observed in men has largely disappeared, with women in the 50–64 age group now statistically tied and younger women far outpacing their male peers. The convergence of lung cancer incidence below age 65 underscores that historical female advantage in smoking-related cancers has eroded.

The racial disparities documented in this report are stark and persistent. AIAN populations experience the highest mortality across multiple cancer types, and Black individuals continue to face substantially elevated death rates for potentially preventable or screen-detectable cancers. Lower stage at diagnosis and differential access to guideline-concordant care — compounded by higher poverty rates — point to structural barriers rather than biological differences as the primary drivers of these gaps.

The pandemic-era interruption of cancer care constitutes an additional concern. The large deficit in 2020 diagnoses was concentrated among asymptomatic, early-stage disease, and the lack of a compensatory "catch-up" in 2021 data (except for breast cancer) suggests genuine delays in detection with possible downstream effects on stage distribution and survival. Published modeling of 4,000–7,000 excess colorectal cancer deaths through 2040 illustrates the time scale on which these consequences may unfold.

The favorable trends in childhood and adolescent cancer survival represent a sustained achievement of pediatric oncology, with 5-year survival now exceeding 85%. Nonetheless, incidence continues to rise slowly in adolescents, warranting continued etiologic investigation.

---

## Limitations

This report has several important limitations acknowledged in the source manuscript. Estimated case and death counts for 2025 are model-based, three- to four-year forward projections; they cannot substitute for observed incidence and mortality rates for tracking temporal change. The projection methodology has been updated periodically, most recently in 2021, limiting the comparability of estimates across annual editions. The models are sensitive to abrupt fluctuations in observed data and cannot account for unanticipated changes in detection or clinical practice.

Racial and ethnic misclassification in medical records and death certificates systematically undercounts cancer events in non-White populations. To mitigate this, AIAN incidence rates are confined to Purchased/Referred Care Delivery Area counties, a restriction that excludes roughly one third of the AIAN population residing in urban areas. Broad racial and ethnic groupings mask heterogeneity within categories; combined AAPI data, for instance, obscure markedly worse outcomes among Pacific Islander individuals. The absence of sexual orientation and gender identity data in cancer surveillance completely precludes analysis of the LGBTQ+ population.

---

## Conclusion

U.S. cancer mortality continues to decline, yielding a 34% reduction relative to the 1991 peak and approximately 4.5 million deaths averted. These gains, however, are shadowed by rising incidence among younger and middle-aged adults — especially women — and by entrenched racial disparities that confer mortality rates two to three times higher among AIAN and Black populations for numerous cancers. Sustained and equitable progress will require greater investment in prevention and expanded access to high-quality screening and treatment, with particular attention to AIAN, Black, and other underserved communities.
